blocks.x: Let's see, let me check this. Testing one, two, three. Say something. Hello, man. What's your name? Okay, it's going all right. This is an interview recorded in seminar room number two of the Howard Tilton Memorial Library. What's the day's date, Punch? What's the day's date, Punch? Today is the 20th, isn't it? 20th of August, 1959. And what's your full name anyway? We ought to get that on the tape.
My first, my real full name is Anis Burton.
And you're better known as Punch Miller.
Oh, yeah. Yeah, yeah.
Bill has already got that stuff about your name, huh?
No, he didn't get that.
Oh, I thought you told him about that on tape.
He said about Punch Miller. I don't know. I don't think I did. No, I didn't tell him about Anis Burton. I'm pretty sure I didn't.
Yeah, well, let me see. Where were you born?
Racism Museum.
And what year? We've got that down.
18 and 94. May 10th.

Yeah, Oddfellas Day, that's right. You don't have to look over towards the microphone or anything. Don't worry about it. We'll just put it right halfway in between us and we'll just talk like we ordinarily do. How did you get started in the music business?

Well, now that's the funny thing. We all, the older parents and things had a big band out there. They got a bunch of new instruments. So everyone that had a son or grandson or anything like that, well, they just give them the old instruments, see? And I don't know, I was lucky enough to come out pretty good. At first it started me on the bass drum. I started to blow in the baritone, it gave me that, I played it pretty good, so they gave me the cornet. And I took the cornet and made good history. Of course I wasn't reading music, but I played everything I could whistle.
And what about the other people in the band, the old people?
Well, the old people all died out. Were they readers? Yeah, they readers readers. The most of them. The most of them was.
Did anybody play any jazz, what you'd call jazz today in that band?
Well, it was on the same order of this.
So they were playing jazz when you were a little boy in Raceland?
Well, exactly what you called it, Dixieland, isn't it? Mm-hmm. Yeah, that's what they were playing.
And how were the people that were playing Dixieland when you were a little boy? Yeah. Have they been playing that kind of music before you think?
Before I was grown?
Before you were grown.

Well yeah, that's all I come up on it. That's all I, you know, nothing about. Until the bop come out and I started playing a little bit of that, but I was never crazy about it, you know. I just tried it out and played it. But I always did play my Dixieland.
I like it. I wondered about that. I just wondered, if those guys weren't readers they must have been playing something pretty close to Dixieland

jazz before you ever bought it. Yeah. But I'll tell you one thing about it. The most they played was like marches. See, they learned a lot of marches. They didn't know a lot of play pieces like banana peeling and all that stuff way back there, you know. Oh, you're beautiful. They played all that kind of stuff. But the most stuff they did play was marches.
Would they be six eighths or two four?
Six eighths.
Mostly six eighths? Yeah. Well I've often wondered if you could really swing in a six eighth march.
Well I've got to slow it down a bit and cut it, cut it up you know. You've got to cut it like a whole note where you make either one half or two half notes out of it.
Did those fellas teach you anything when you started out?
Well yeah. The man that taught me was named Paul Roja. He was a very good reader.
Paul Roja.
Roja. Paul Roja. He was a nice musician.
And when you started fooling around with bass drum, how old were you?
Well I say, now I can't exactly remember, but I put it around eleven years old.
Uh huh. And then how long did you stay on that?

I stayed on bass drum say like about a year. And I picked up the baritone, carried it along about six months. And we was playing pretty regular, see. So the boys on trumpets figured I was pretty strong and they told me to take a trumpet there, a half out more. So I took the trumpet and I played it mighty good.
And what kind of music and songs did you hear out in the country there?
Well, it was like I tell you, that Beautiful Doll was good, Take Your Hands Away, and a lot of other, but I can't think of the name of them now.
What is Take Your Hands Away?
A song.
I don't remember that.

Take your hands away, take your hands away, you don't know who's watching you, so take your hands away. That's the way it goes. There's a lot more to it, but I mean that's the way it goes. I'm a big fan of the blues. And I'll tell you a song, two more numbers that just come to me. Grizzly Bear and Everybody Doing It. See, I know all them old numbers, I know them good.
And they were playing those when you were a kid?
Yeah.
The Grizzly Bear, what is that about?

Listen my honey do while I try to show to you the dance that called the Grizzly Bear. Hug up close to watch baby, throw your heel toward the ceiling, that will give you funny feelings. Snug up close to watch baby, clip your eyes and do some nothing, something nice is going to happen. Hug up close to watch baby, swing her everywhere, show your love and doubting how you go to Buffalo. Doing the Grizzly Bear. That's what he was singing them days.
I like that. Yeah, that's good. I know there's another one about Grizzly Bear. Lord if you can't help me please don't help me.
Oh yeah, I remember that. I remember that whole piece.
Yeah, because sometimes you get things like that confused. You want to know which is which. So that's how you got started out. And you said there's plenty of blues out there. Would they

sing the blues much out there? No, that's one thing about it. I didn't do much singing then. You just play. I didn't start singing until I come in New Orleans. And who would sing out there? Well nobody unless there's somebody out there dancing go to singing. You know what I mean? That's the only way you're singing them times.
Well what about the people who were working on just sweeping up around the house, you know,

cleaning up? Would they sing? Oh yeah, there's a lot of singing, cleaning up and going on like that. Yeah, there's a lot of that. What kind of work did you do out there? Plow, make sugarcane. Did you get lonesome and sing when you plowed? Yeah, I always was lonesome on the farm. Yeah. I always wanted to leave that day for my little kid. Wanted to leave that place. I don't know why but there never was in my mind to stay there. Would you sing when you were lonely plowing or cutting can? Yeah, I'd be singing some kind of blues or something to myself, you know. A lot of people did that? Yeah.
Would you sing in a gang when you were cutting can? Or doing anything?

Man, pretty much everybody would be singing. Yeah. And what would you sing? Do you remember any of those numbers? Well, I can't remember nothing. It's been so long ago. But I'd sing something about I want to leave this town, this place, and find a better home, something like that. I sing or something
like that. Yeah, there are a lot of good work songs, you know, like that, man. A lot of good work songs, you know. Oh yeah. You sing while you're working, all different kinds.

Yeah. You hear the man, Bob Keno, he sing a song, and I liked it too. He sing a song about, been a long, long, long, long, long, long, long, long, long time. I ain't had nothing in, ain't had nothing, ain't had nothing in a long time. And I always used to like to hear him sing that. I don't know why, but there was nothing to it named Johnny Lewis. Johnny Lewis? Yeah, old man Johnny Lewis. He was a boy old man, but he used to sing that.
And what did he do? Was he just working in Raceland?
Yeah, he was one of the farmers. One of them good old farmers.
Let me turn off the machine a sec. Remember any other songs that the farmers used to sing out there?

I don't know. I can't remember knowing about words. I just, I don't know, I just know a little hair of them, but I don't know about words. You saw it, you say, ooh, I whip my girl with a single tree. You might have yet a hollering, don't murder poor me. See them old, them old time songs, but that's what they used to sing. That's what they used to sing.
What was that? I whip my woman with a single tree?

Yeah. And you might hear a hollering, please don't murder me. And say the baddest man, no, came but one man on the road out here, that's Buddy Mac Miller and he don't come here. All that kind of stuff, see? He used to sing. And did they take any of those things and put them into jazz tunes? Well, no. I mean, no, like them first ones I told you, but you couldn't put that in. I mean you could, but you had to sit down a good while to fix that out, you know.
Yeah, I thought maybe they took some of those songs that they sang while they were working and

made them into jazz tunes. Well no, they didn't in them times. Dick, I'll tell you why, there wasn't nobody there to fix nothing like that, you know. Now he did, I'd pick up on something like that and
make something out of it, you know. Well what about in the churches? What went on now?

Well they used to sing hymns, you know, and real good hymns too. Remember the names of any of them? Well, the boys I know, the best one I used to like, I mean, was, was, uh, His Eyes Is On The Sparrow and I Know He's Watching Me. And he doesn't know, but oh how I loved Jesus, because he first loved me. And neither of them regard to thee. Well them kind of hymns, you know, I remember and still go for them. Much Long Me To Hymns? Yeah, yeah, a lot of long me to hymns. But I never could keep up with them good. What about these tunes that the bands play now? Well these hymns I mean that the bands play now? Well that did come out late, these late years, like when the synths go marching and all that, that come out these late years. But Close To Walk, I think that's back, a little bit back. Glory Land? What about over in the Glory Land? Oh yeah, that's back, that's way back. And uh…

And we ain't got no water any. Yeah, we can turn it off if you want to go get a drink, sure. No, but I mean I want to take a Alka-Seltzer. Sure. Well… Did they have any instruments in the church, Bodge? Nothing but piano. Nothing but piano. Well nowadays you see trombones and everything at church.
Oh yeah. Guitar? Sure. But them days, you know, nothing but the piano. I mean way back now, I'm speaking about way back.
What about guitar players? Did they have any guitar players out there?
In church? Oh yeah, they had them and a boy named Joseph Phillip. Boy, he could pick a guitar. My God. I never heard nobody play a guitar like him.
I wonder what ever happened to him.
He's right over here in, wait now I'll call it, Semio, Florida. Not Semio, no. Boy that place has got a funny name. Kasemi. Kasemi. Kasemi, Florida. That's a, we call it a cattle town.
He'd be easy to find over there you think?
Yeah, I'll write him. He played bass now and guitar.
Do you remember if he used a pick or did he use finger style?
He'd pick. Picking.
Pick with his hands? With his fingers. Yeah, with his fingers and then he could rap too.
Yeah, yeah. Oh he was a guitar man.
Oh yeah, well he'd be worth looking up.
And I'll tell you another fella I worked with a long time. Of course we all call him Rooster. But his name is Lonnie Johnson. You heard of him.
Oh yeah.

Well me and him play together with guitar and trumpet up and down Bollyfoot long time ago. It's guitar and trumpet. Lonnie Johnson. But we all call him Rooster at home. Well where is he from? He's from uh somewhere out from Memphis. Not on, not in Memphis.
Mm-hmm.
Out from Memphis. A little small place. I believe it's Tennessee City or something like that. Mm-hmm.
Yeah. And he uh used to hang around the Bayou Lafourche area though. Yeah. That's right.

See with me a lot of us hang around that dick I tell you. See out there on them farms if you didn't work you couldn't stay there see. But when you get on by him out there on that levee couldn't nobody bother you. Nothing but the sheriff and if you just tell him you're just laying off or you're sick or something ask you where you're staying you tell him you live in Greentown or Morristown where he couldn't bother you. Couldn't bother you unless you live on this side on them planations see. Mm-hmm. All the way. So we didn't do nothing but hang on there and live and play music week like three nights a week and lived on it too.
You get much money for those three nights?
Yeah. Why do we get a dollar and a half? Some good people give us two dollars you know.
That's per night?
Oh yeah. That's good money though. Two dollars a night you could get. Yeah. You know a dollar, dick a dollar could buy you and have groceries all the week. Mm-hmm.
And how uh how many bands did they have out there around Raceland?
Two. Three. By the Zelmer had a band, Raceland had a band, and Bui, Louisiana had a band.
And what were the names of the bands?
Well they called it the Bui Band, By the Zelmer Band, and the Raceland Band. That's all they called it.
And who played in the band there?

Well now Mike Taylor had the band in the Bui. The name was Spencer Taylor but everybody called him Mike. And I can't think of all the fellas, they were the Sawmill guys, they called it Sawmill. Yeah. They didn't play until on Sundays you know. Couldn't play no other day. And that fella that came to teach me, Paul Rosi had a band in Baudis Elmo. And a fella named Tooker, I forget, Tooker, real name, but he had the band that raised it, the old men bands. And Johnny Hills, he was the boy that took over the young boy's band, but he never could play. He never could play. So they gave it to me see. But I didn't stay there. And I was after, when I got 16, 17, I went on endowment. When you were 17?
Yeah.

But I put it up though. It was going from 18 to 35. And I put it up. If you look it up, you find out I was born in 1894. But I was born, and I have to tell you the truth, but I was born in 1895 see. But after I put it up to 1894 I let it stay there see. But I was 17, I ain't no joke about that. And so out there how big would those bands be, the different ones? The band we had must have had about, I'll tell you. We had Johnny Hill, Claiborne Roy, Esau Lewis, David Lewis, Oscar Shields, Joseph Pugh, Sullivan Pugh, Joseph Phillip, and what they named, Dukes, Arthur Dukes, and myself, Daniel Hadley, that's 11, and Kemp Hadley, Holly Taylor. Oh man, they had about 18 pieces. Gee, that's a big band. Yeah.
And what instruments would those guys play?

Well they had about four trombones, two baritones, two tubas, three altos, and they had two snare drum players, one bass drum. They didn't have no saxophones, and oh that's right, they had two clarinets, but they didn't have no saxophone.
What did Joseph Phillip play?
Joseph Phillip? He played tuba. He played tuba in the big band, you know, but he played guitar and bass violin, and if we played dance, we had an orchestra too, see?
Oh yeah.
Yeah, sure.
How big were these other bands?

What, the orchestra? No, at the different places like Bowie. Oh Bowie, well they had, them fellas had a good large band too. They must have about twelve pieces, and Bowie, the Zelmer had about, I'd say eleven or twelve. All that was a big band.
We might as well get those names and instruments together in Raceland. Who played which instrument?
Oh well, Johnny Hill played trumpet, I played trumpet, Esau Lewis played trumpet, and what are those four trumpets? Johnny, myself, Esau Lewis, and Holly Taylor.
Why don't you put them down? That's right there. Oh that's right.

That's right. And Phillip played tuba and Oscar Shields played tuba. David Lewis on bass drum, Holly Taylor on snare drum. Let me see now, Bluff, his name is Oscar, yeah Oscar, yeah Bluff played alto, Claiborne Royal played alto, and David Lewis played alto. Three alto. Three alto. And Daniel Hadley played crannet and his brother played crannet, Oscar Hadley.
Now what about trombones?
Trombones, get to them now. Yeah. Sullivan Pugh, Joseph Pugh, them was trombone player. Them brothers, Sullivan Pugh and Joseph Pugh.
Did they have one more? How many did you say? Four trombones or three?

No they had three. I'm trying to think this boy would die. Claiborne Royal. Claiborne Royal, he played trombone. That's three, see? They tried to make it three in a row. One row three, another row three, another row three, and another row three. See like that, you know, that's where they reached the parade. They used to parade like two in a line, three in a...
What about baritone horns? Did we name them?

Yeah, I called three baritones. I don't remember. I told you Arthur Dukes, I don't remember. I don't remember. That's right, they had two baritone and an alto walk together. And two altos and a trombone walk together. Arthur Dukes played baritone and Oscar Shields. Oscar Shields.
Yeah, good. That must be it, drums, tubas, trumpets, clarinets.
Two snare drums.
Now in those days, what instrument went first in a parade? Cornet. Cornet walked in front.
Oh no, the tuba walked in front.
The tuba in front.

Yeah, the tuba walked in front. I thought you meant what instrument was leading. No. See this boy, Esau Lewis, he played what you call an E flat trumpet. And we played B flat trumpet. See he couldn't play much but what he played, because you heard first, way up over everybody. Way up high.
He played the melody?
Hmm?
Did he play the melody? Did he play the lead?
Yeah, he played the lead, sure. But like if I'm playing, da da da da da da da, would he make this, see like that, see, up over me.
But when they were walking, who would come first? The tubas and then what?

The tubas, the baritone, the alto, no. Yeah, tubas, the trombone for his ninth. But it was the tuba, the baritone, the trombone, the alto, the trumpets, then the clarinets, then the drums. That's the reason.
They've changed it all around, man.
Oh yeah.
Well you can see a good reason for putting the trombones in front.
Oh yeah, on that kind of that.
Yeah, they might hit somebody with that slide.

Yeah, but the way they used to walk, they never touched nobody. Them guys that used to play the trombone like they play them now. They play them, I mean, like that now. But them guys, they play that horn right across. After we were here, everybody.
And they were using slides.
Huh?
They were using slides.
Well, two slides and one vowel. Mm-hmm.
Now did they have any bands from the neighboring towns come in there?

Well, the buoy band would come get after us and the Zellema band would come to have, well, what do they used to call that? They used to call it a book and things like that. They used to call it a band Kunze. We'd play our little stuff, they'd play over there, they'd play over there, but that buoy band was the best.
Did they produce any men that have become famous since then?
No.
They just stood around there, I guess, huh? That's all. That's all.
It was a man come here, I never seen him, but it was the son of this man I told you about, Johnny Lewis.
Mm-hmm.

Well, he saw Lewis and David Lewis, them his two sons too. But he had an older son come here, played bass trombone. They said he's the talk of New Orleans. He used to play with this buddy of old. His name was Bobo, Bobo. Called him Bobo. But I believe, I don't know what his first name was, Lewis, but I know everybody called him Bobo. And they said he was a tuba playing man out of the world. But I never heard no talk of him here in New Orleans.
That's something.
That's way back down, Buddy Bowling days, see? Mm-hmm. Yeah.
Did Buddy Bowling ever come out there?
Well, I don't know.
You wouldn't know my band might go there.

No. I didn't never get to see him. I don't mean I wasn't old enough to see him, but I just never, I'll tell you the man I first seen when I was kind of getting on my feet with Trumpet, the first man I seen, I ain't gonna lie, it was Bunk Johnson. I seen him on my excursion pass our home recently, going to Homer, Louisiana, and I went on that excursion and I saw him play. First time. And I didn't ever see Joe Oliver until I went to Chicago.
That's a funny thing, you can live in the same town with people and never hear him.
Right. Well, I mean Dick, I didn't come to New Orleans until I left the Army. That was 1919. See what I mean?
Yeah.
I got discharged, instead of going back to Riesling, I come right on to New Orleans.
Well before the war, did you ever come into New Orleans at all?
Yeah, like we make a sugar grinder. I'll come in and buy clothes and things, but go right back.
Did you hear any music?
No, never did, not in them time. No, I'll come in and get my clothes on Ramport Street and go right on back. Never did stay here to get no music.
How did Bunk play when you first heard him? Did he sound like his records is what I mean?
Yeah, he sounded just the same to me. He sounded just like them records.
How loud was he when you heard him in person?
Oh, he's pretty strong then. Yeah, he was strong, yeah.
Do you remember any of that?
Louder. Yeah, one piece I'll never forget he played, Alexander's Ragtime Band. He could play that all day for me.
Well, we'll play you the record of that sometime.
Yeah, Alexander's Ragtime Band. He really played that. But Dick, what I want to ask you, what do you think about how long you think Rock and Roller lasts?
Oh, I don't know. It can't last much longer.

Well, in my mind, the way I figured out, if any little thing different come in with, I mean it got to be noisy, got to be flashy, you know, stuff. It'll knock it out. But Cha Cha ain't going to knock it out.
No.

Not that. See Cha Cha is good music, but it ain't got no, what these young people wanted, that noise and stuff and flashy stuff, you see. That's what killed them off, see. Of course, Dixieland, don't care what come out, he's going to hang around, you know, and it might get famous again. Of course, Dixieland is a standard kind of music, you know, a standard.
Well, there'll always be people playing the blues, I figure.
Oh, as long as you live there. See, Rock and Roll ain't got butt blues.
How many blues pickers did they have out there, you say, around your neighborhood? Just get to them.

Well, they had Joseph Phillip, Roy Lonnie Johnson. Well, they had a lot more of them, but didn't compare with them, see. It was right smart to get to our players. You could see guys walking them down, the liver would get down on the shoulder all the time. You want me to get in touch with Joseph Phillip?
Yeah.
How about right away?
Yeah, that's fall. I know a guy would like to look him up, maybe take a trip over there. Yeah.
Yeah. Well, he's the type of man to find, because he can tell you a lot. He's an older fella. He's older than I am, a couple of years.
But what about your army service? Did you play any music then?

Yeah, I was bugle. I played in the brass band and I played in the dance orchestra. Didn't I tell you about it? I used to go along and watch a fella named Chiff and the brass band parade, watch his fingers. I was fast enough to make the same thing he'd be making, but he told me that wasn't no good. He said, the best thing for you to do is to, I know a little music then, but I didn't know no marches, because Port Royalty was showing me pretty good. But I couldn't get them marches down like I wanted, see. After I come into getting them marches down, well I didn't have no more trouble. But anyhow, they made a car for Buell out of me. I got a little funny story to tell you about that. They had us all lined up, you know, in the Army. When I first went there now we hadn't got our Army clothes yet. So Sergeant standing up there with four Buells hanging on this side and four on this side, talking to us, telling us what the Army rules and things. So he said everybody's staying in line. I forgot he said that. So I walked out of line. I said, look here, Sarge. I said, if a man blow one of them Buells there, I said, that's his job? That's his job. He said, we fall back in line. So he come down off the stand and gave me Buells and said, let's see, can you blow it? I said, oh I can blow it. I said, if you blow something I'll blow it. So he blew it, I can't get him up, but I blew it right behind him. He said, oh yeah, you can make it. And that was my job, see, blowing bugle. So he made a couple of them and I teach the other fellas. Same fella I call us, and Oscar Sheehy, he comes to the same camp I come. I teach them how to blow bugle. I put on a little, what you call it, the captain wanted to hear it. He heard us blowing three Buells with our hand, like that you know. So he called us one night about nine o'clock and made us come up there and made me get the other boys and show them how we do that. And we show them, and I was solid. Yeah. I played in the brass band, the string band, and the jazz, I mean, and the Buell. They're pretty nice in the army. And you know, I was called to leave there, they didn't tell me that till after. I was called to leave there over five times. But they sent somebody else, never sent me. I was called to leave there. Where's Chip from? Chip from up on the river, yeah. Him and Kidora come from the same home.
You say Chiff's been dead. Three years. Three years now. I never met him.
You never did?
What did he play you say?
Trumpet. He's a mighty good trumpet player too. Good musician I mean. Good musician.
And did he play any other instrument?
No. A lot of people don't know I played with Celestan but I did, I played with Celestan, Goodwild. But Jack Kerr was my main man you know.
What did you play, second trumpet with Celestan?
Yeah, second trumpet, that's right.
Was that a brass band job or?
Well I played in a brass band on a parade but I played, I'm talking about his dance orchestra now. I did some of the feature trumpet for him.
Yeah. And when was that?
I'd say in 22. Right in there.
And who was his second trumpet before you?
Oh, let me see who he is. At least no shots come after me. That was an old man, I forget who it was now. But shots come after me you know. Didn't I think I killed after shots eh?

Either him or Ricard, I can't remember which. They were both in there and I can never remember which is which. So let's see, you were in the army and who were some of the other New Orleans guys in the army with you?

Well, just Oscar Shields. There was about the three of us, oh no, what is I'm talking about? Clowns Todd, Chiff, there's a triumphant player named Ben. Ben, Ben something, he from off the river to a real Creole fellow. Ben, he named Ben, I can't think of his first name.
They call him Ben or something like that?

Yeah, Ben. His name must have been Benjamin but they called him Ben. But anyhow Clowns Todd was on piano, Chiff and me was on trumpets, and this Ben man, I can't think of his name. To tell you the truth I think the Moosef was from New Orleans but I just can't think of him now. But the Moosef was right out of New Orleans.
Well how did Clowns Todd play? What kind of piano?
He played nice, he played really nice.
Readin' piano player?
Yeah, he's a pretty good reader.
Did he play ragtime tunes or blues or what?

Yeah, he played all that. Now that's a man doing some singing. He did very smart singing. But I didn't think much of his voice, I don't want to critic him or nothing, but I didn't think so much of his voice. But he used to sing though. And he's a lively fellow, he's long clothed for God.
Did you ever know Hank Benson? Sure, Hank Benson, trombone player. He worked with you, that's right. Yeah. It wasn't him on trombone in the Army though, huh?
No, he wasn't in the Army with me. If he was, I didn't know him then.
It was another Ben that played trombone then.
Paul Ben.
Oh, Paul Ben.
Paul Ben. Paul Ben, that's his name. Yeah. Paul Ben. I knew it would come to me.
I see. So, did they feature, around that time, did they feature any tunes like Maple Leaf Rag or Frog Leg Rag where you were?
Yeah, Maple Leaf was the famous, but I don't know, but Frog Legs. Climax. Climax. They played there. And this, what's that about the leaf you call it, Silver Leaf.
Silver Leaf Rag. Yeah. Rose Leaf I've heard out too. Well, they had a Silver Leaf too.
Mm-hmm. Yeah.
I don't know.
And the other thing was out then in them days, Panama Rag. Mm-hmm. Panama Rag, we played that. High Society, we played all them kind of numbers. That's when you were first getting started.
Yeah. Awesome. When did they start playing Make Me a Pallet on the floor? Oh, that was before my time.
But I played it, but they started that before my day. Oh, yeah.
What about Tiger Rag? When did they start playing that?

Well, I'm gonna tell her, I got used to Tiger Rag right there with Jack Kerr in New Orleans. We the first one started singing Tiger Rag. Jack Kerr band. First band started singing it, Hold That Tiger. Yeah.
Well they used to sing something else about Jack Kerr in there too, didn't they?
Well yeah, Jack Kerr had a daughter on the water selling pork chops too for a quarter. Yeah.
Yeah, well that fits right in. That's a melody that fits in.
Yeah.
Now what was the first band you played with here?
Ernest Johnson. You know Dave Johnson? Played the drum. He played, he was a, well you remember that Sunday you gave me two dollars on there by
Carrier Boots?
Yeah. Well he was playing the bass drum that Sunday.
Dave Bailey. Yeah.

Yeah, Dave Bailey. Yeah, well that's Ernest Johnson's brother. See? They must be half brother. But anyhow, they were always there, we were out in front of town there on Chippy Ward in St. Thomas. That's where they lived then. And what made me go out there, it was a boy out in the army, what he did now, I forget his name, but his mother lived out there and he told me to come and I could stay with him. That's how we were good friends in the army see? So he brought me there and they really treated me nice. I lived good. Well that's how I joined that band. He went to Ernest Johnson and Barberman see? And I got in that band there. Well Jack Carey was on the Avatar one Sunday and he heard me play. He used to steal for guys like that you know, so he'd find out where I lived and come out there and talk to him and I'd like to come back, you know back of town anyhow. So I come on and join Jack Carey. And I played with Jack a long climb, man. There was one fella that I really wish would have did something like a record or some kind of something before he died. I liked him so much, that was Buddy Petit. Oh yeah. Ain't got nothing of him.
Well nobody's found it yet. I've heard talk of his record. He's supposed to have made, but you never know.
But I mean, who should have it?
Little Dad, you might ask Little Dad. Little Dad what he plays? Banjo.
Yeah I know him, what come of him?
He's living up near where Willie Humphrey lives.
Yeah, that short fella.

Yeah. Well anyway, he's supposed to know about it. And various people have talked about it, but I don't know. You can't always tell what to believe, you know. That's right. You heard so many stories about him.
That's right.
But who was this Ernest Johnson there?
Ernest Johnson, a bass player.
And who did he have in his band?

Well they had, I don't know what this tipping guy name on trombone, there's a tip when he wore, a dark fella. And Dave on drum and me on trumpet, well he was different clarinet players. You never had the same clarinet players, you know. George Boyd played with us a while. What's the name, Little Pill? Cripple Pill. Yeah. Let's see, did they have a guitar at the band?
A banjo? Yeah, a banjo. You know the banjo play out there, I forget.

Oh that's been so long. Oh yeah. But a guy from front of town. Oh yeah. When did the banjo start being used with bands? Well they were using guitar when I first come here. Then banjos jumped in there all at once. And they lasted a pretty good while you know. They lasted a pretty good while. When did they start using the tubas with the dance bands?
I wondered about that too.

Well I don't know about here. Well in Chicago I was playing with a boy named Francois Mosley and the other fella named William Hilliard. And I was in the twenties and he was playing tuba with us. And he played so, man you thought it was a bass violin. He didn't play no louder than the orchestra played. Except that tuba right down there. But William Hilliard, they called him Bill Hilliard.
That's right, he's on the record with you I think. Yeah, yeah.

I believe. Well who was with Jack Carey in there? Jack Carey, myself, George Foster, Little Chinese, George Boyd. Well I'll tell you about that now. They had a boy, I don't know if he's Kent the Old Man Robichaux or not, but we used to call him Robichaux and he claimed he's a relation to Old Man Robichaux, he played violin at the Larry Theater. He's real light with nice hair. Well he played clarinet with us at the Moes. Played what?
Clarinet?
Clarinet, clarinet.
I never heard of him.

Robichaux, well anybody around here tell him, he's younger than any of us too. But I do believe he did. We all called him Robichaux, see because I went to his house one time to get him to play. And he said that we should whistle for musicians, like that. So his old mother, somebody come to the door and said, what dog are you calling? I said Robichaux. Boy I point up, I said Robichaux. So he come to the door and say old man, I said yeah I am, I said I'm feeling no mind. So you know it's one of them things you know. And Lorenzo Stahl, I'm just putting some stuff in now, Lorenzo Stahl, he was with Jack Carey, he was playing manager. So some man wanted us to go to Birmingham to play two nights, pay all the expenses and give us a hundred dollars a man a night. So Lorenzo was so funny you know. He asked Jack, he said, Jack how much you going to give him, talking about Robichaux. Jack said I'm going to give him two hundred dollars. He said man give me some of that money. I said boy all that money, boy sitting up there playing I Will Follow Where They Lead It. So you know I don't want to like that.
Boy he made Robichaux for a boy cry like a baby. That's true for me to God ever. Did you read with those bands like Ernest Johnson? No. Did you read with Jack Carey?

No. Uh uh. I ain't going to lie. Yeah, well nobody was, well that's good. Tell you about one thing happened. A white lady right down the bottom of the tea room, what's the name of that room, it was up your town here. Yeah. She had a piano copy of her song. It's the truth. And she brought that piano copy and asked us what we played and I played it down. I'll tell you what it was. That piece that I'll never get along as I left. And they couldn't follow me but you know the bass and the guitar that's hitting along with me and she thought it was mighty wonderful. She said I think that's nice. But the other boy just now they couldn't play.
That's nothing could be finer than being Carolina in the Mar.
Yeah, that's the name of it.
Yeah, I remember that piece. Well now who were the bands that played mostly society music, just reading, no Dixieland?

Well Tuxedo, very little reading they had though, I ain't going to lie. I'll tell you the band that had the real readers in it, P-Rong, A.J. P-Rong. Did they play any Dixieland? They played Dixieland but they played a lot of the music, beautiful numbers and things you know? Yeah. Yeah.
And what about Celestan's Tuxedo? What would he feature?

Well they had, I remember they played Moise Dixieland see? He played Moise Dixieland. Of course he'd know a song from way back though, that helped him see? He played solid Dixieland. How long were you with Jack Carey?
Let me see. I bought John Jack in 20.

And I would have stayed with him all the time. And I would have stayed with him all the time. But Joy Boyer, Walter Preston, Joe Gable, Chani Foster. And them guys kept forcing me to quit Jack and let's get us own band. They did that a long time before I quit. But I said, well all right, I said we're going to put the band in your name. Kept on- I didn't want to quit Jack. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. They just kept forcing me to quit Jack and let's get us our own band. They did that a long time before I quit. But I said, well all right, we're going to put the band in your name. I didn't want to quit Jack, but they did and so I just went on to quit. But we didn't ever fall out. So I got my own band. And we did good. But I wouldn't think about doing anything like that myself.
Why did they want to quit Jack?
I don't know myself, but I guess they just figured if we, I don't know, there wasn't nothing wrong with him. I don't know. I didn't see nothing wrong.
Well now, when you quit Jack Carey, who came in on trombone with your band?
E.D. Morris. Right on. I'm right in. I see. I said, George Boyd went and got him right away.
And that would be around the time you were playing with Celestan then, huh?

I don't know how it mixed up, but I wasn't with Celestan then. I must have been with Celestan in 19 and going into 20, see. Because I went with Jack Carey from, I don't know how that thing messed up now. Yeah. From, I can't see because I left in 27. That's what got me positive.
Well you had your own band up until the time you left. That's right.
That's right.
So it had to be Jack Carey before your band.
That's right.
And then Celestan must have been before that.
No, yeah, yeah, yeah, because Ernest Johnson was the first one. But I didn't play with Ernest Johnson for more than two or three months.
See.
I didn't stay there long at all.
And Jack Carey heard you though while you were with Ernest Johnson.
Oh yeah, yeah.
And when did Celestan pick up on you?

Well Celestan picked up on me one night. I went to Italian Hall on Esplanade Street. Well I wasn't playing that night and I just went there and I wanted to blow something. He had never seen me. And I played a little bit and he asked me who I was working with. I told him well I just wasn't working with nobody at that particular time. So he said well come to the high school. And I went to the high school. And he played a lot of old time stuff. Well I played you know I played the second trumpet right behind him. And he told me, he said get up and blow something and let the boys hear you. And I got up and blow it and especially that tramo player, he's crazy about me. Baby, what's his name, Baby?
I know who you mean. He's an old man now, lives uptown. Yeah, yeah. Up around Calton. On Edinburgh he used to live. Is that the guy Baby Ridgely? Baby Ridgely, yeah.
Baby Ridgely, yeah. And I didn't play with them too long. Was Ridgely?
Was Ridgely a strict reader or did he play by ear too?
Well he read like the devil's lots. Maybe a few pieces he played by ear but he always had that music up there.
Did they have any clarinets or saxophones there?
Yeah, they had good clarinets players.
Who was clarinet with Celestine?
I'm trying to think. The last one I know was this little fella, what we tell me this now. What do you know, the hump in his back? That's the last one I know played with. Not the cripple fella?
Yeah, Peele.
Peele played with fellow Stan?
Yeah. Same time you were.
Yeah. Yeah, Peele was in the band when I got there. Yeah. But he had a better clarinet player than Peele though, but I can't figure who he was, no. He had several of them.
He had Willard Toomey at one time, did you know him?
Yeah, then after I heard he had Willie Humphreys a while.
Yeah, and let me see, there was another one I can't think of. Well, let's see, Paul Barnes I think played clarinet. Yeah.
Carrier. Yeah, way down, he lived way down.
Sidney Carrier, did you know him?
Sidney Carrier, yeah, I know him but I can't, you know, I'm a member, but I know Paul Barnes good.
Yeah. Well, they were all in there around that time, a little later maybe.
Mm-hmm.
Who did Celestan have in the rhythm section?

Well, that lady on piano, Clown's sister, Camilla Todd, is that her name? Mm-hmm. Now, who was on bass? Chester Zadis played bass with him, why? But before that he had George Foster, that's right. He was- He was-
He was the same one was with Jack Carey, huh? Yeah, same one.

Same guy. Yeah. And guitar, Tom Benton. Boy, he's getting me back there to think now. I got to think about them kind of fellas, you know, Tom Benton, yeah that was his guitar player. Played with him a long time.
Did he have a good drummer then?
Yeah, this guy played a drum with him. Bill Matthews.
Oh yeah.
I still played a drum with him. Dick, you sure are calling me back. Yeah, now you're making me get some stuff.
Well we've been working on it long enough.
Mm-hmm.
How long have I known you now? It's been a long time. You know what I mean?
Yeah.
Ever since I've been back. When did you come back? No, not ever since I've been back. Yeah.
I went to work at, no I'll tell you where you know me, I just had gotcha down at Larry's. Yeah. But I hadn't been here long. Yeah.
I'm trying to remember what year it was when you first came back.
Oh, twenty, fifty-six. Fifty-six.
You got it. Mm-hmm. So, let's see. You had different guys in your band, I know you had a lot of different drummers I know it told me.
Yeah, yeah, yeah, I couldn't keep regular drummers.
But I didn't have but two, three. China?

Three. Three. Arnel Matoyer. What's his name? Arnel? No, Arnal something. A little short, short fella, a stomach on him like that. Tell me he's a policy writer now. He's downtown. Arnal. Arnal. But not Matoyer there, that was a trumpet player. Yeah. But he named Arnal DePaz.
Oh, I didn't know he was downtown.
Yeah, DePaz, Arnal DePaz. Well, but he wasn't my first drummer. See, Chinese kept on messing up and I used to have to go like the devil and get somebody, see.
He'd blow you up, Chinese?
Yeah, he used to blow me up a lot of times. But I tell you who played me a long time, Happy Goldston. He took Chinese plays, see. I kept him when I got him. That's before he went to the tuxedo.
Well, Chinese was with the tuxedo.
Chinese was a good drummer, but Chinese would get high like that and mess you up, man.
Did Paul Barber never play with you? Well, yeah.
Paul Barber, I don't want to tell that to him. Paul Barber, yeah, when he first came back from Lewis he joined me.
I thought maybe he played with you in those days, in years gone by. Before? Yeah, with Eddie Marsh and George E. Bush.

Yeah, that's when he played with me. That's when he played with me, before I ever left here. He had been to Chicago with Lewis and he said something, he got slow in his foot or something, I don't know what was wrong. But he left Chicago and come here, see. And he joined my band and played with me. Until one night we was playing with some white boys back, way back off Porter Street. Back, I believe Galvis, somewhere around that day. And Paul must have thought he was still up north, you know, trying to flag them girls, see. But I said the boy was watching him. They all knowed me, them white boys. So they called me outside. He said, you better tell that drummer something or you get hype. I said, what's the matter? He said, well, he's, one girl said that he told her he'd gone for a big way and all that old kind of stuff, you know. So they're fixing to get off all that night, see. So what I did, I told him, I said, well you all leave him alone, I bet you don't buy nobody anymore. So I told him about it and he quit that night and then I got gold stuck with me. I said, I got gold stuck with me. Yeah, that man felt fixing to mess up man, completely.
But he know it better, yeah.
But he just thought he could get by with it. He know it better.
Where all the young-
Excuse me, but I've been all over the country and nothing like that was with me. So I always, nowhere up long, be there. I never let nothing like that was with me.
What kind of jobs did y'all play in those days with those different bands?

Well lawn parties was the most. They was going big, middle of the week or any time. And like maybe they called Buddy Petit to go to Bugaloosa Friday and Saturday. They called me to go to Gurpoor, Biloxi Friday and Saturday. They called Rene to go up here in maybe Macomb City or Bad Nourish. But that's how the band made their money. Every band like Saturday and Friday to go off somewhere. Sunday they had to be back here to play these economy halls and advertising and things all like that. Now all day Sunday the band that is not on the streets is out at that lake. The band that wasn't on the street was out on that lake, playing like the devil. I remember sometimes they used to have seven, eight bands out there. And Dick I don't mean far apart. This man got this pavilion here. You got one right over there. And tell you how close together. If they're playing, we have to stay still, people would have to dance by their music. And we play, they dance by our music. That's how close we were together. They had them things built out in the water, you know.
You remember any of the different guys that was playing?
Around what?
At Millenburg out there.
Oh, you mean out on them things?
Yeah, the different other bands.
Well, I'm telling you now, Rene, myself, Buddy Petit be somewhere, Chris Kelly be somewhere. And different bands, you know like that.
What about the white bands? Did they have white bands out there?

Well, they played at Millenburg the most. I mean Spanish food. That's what the most did, they played out that way, see. And we played Millenburg, see. Let me see now. Did you ever play an Irish channel?
Oh yeah, but my God. Did you ever play in the Irish Channel?
Oh yeah, but my God. See, I used to play, I'd sign a contract, I'd finish this Mardi Gras, and sign a contract right there for the next Mardi Gras, for the Buzzards. You ever heard of the Buzzards?
I followed them.

Lord, I used to play for them every year. Buzzards. It was good. I mean, they treat you nice, boy. But in the other way, I remember I could, the only way I got by one time out there, I had to tell them boys who I was and everything. I said, this is Kid Punch. I play for the Buzzards every year. Boy, they're fixing to crucify me. For what? For nothing? They just didn't want you to walk them through that. No business walking through that. That's what that means. Nigga, where you going to walk through? You know where you going? I said, yeah, I live down up here. He said, well, hell, you ain't got no business through here. I said, well, I come to see the man by signing the contract for the Buzzards. I play for the Buzzards every year. So for some reason, this man had a student right across the street, see? And so another boy come up and said, well, there's a man over there. You want to go see him? So I went there. I said, look here. I said, I'm Punch. Kid Punch played for you. He said, oh, yeah, yeah. What's happened? I said, well, I'm trying to get home with the white boy. He's going to whip me up up there. And he come on out of there. I said, god damn, y'all leave that fellow alone. That fellow play music for me every year. Yeah, that's true.
They were pretty rough in the channel, huh?

Oh, yeah, man. It was rough. Well, the Negroes were rough too, partner. Yeah, they was tough too. Dang, man. They had a girl there. They got broke out after me there. And she's going with a waking fellow there. You know what I mean? I didn't know, Dick. And there were about four of them that were going to kill me when we get in that night. We had played at St. Elizabeth Hall up there at Napoleon Avenue. And I'm coming in that night and they're all in the corner. But lucky Johnson was in front of me and Dave and them. And me and Dave and them were back there talking, running out of my mouth, half drunk, you know. So when Ernest got there, they asked him where was I? I said, we're going to kill her that time of tonight. I said, for what? The man said, if you want to be this man's old lady. So Ernest said, oh, no, man. Well, I wouldn't. She's after me, but I had never bothered with her. So they got that thing up and found out she was lying. She's just after me, but she was lying. See, when he got after, she was lying. So I got to be good friends to them. They never bothered me after that.
This was a colored dance?
Yeah, colored dance. You know what she did after that dance? What's that? That woman told me she was going to bring me half a pint to the cooperators and all. And they had poison in it.
Good Lord.

But Lord is good. Something keep on telling me. I put that thing inside my chair right there. And something just kept a whooping me. Don't you touch that bottle. And doggone little fellow took that bottle. Some boy drinks a lot. Say he'd drink anything. Tuck that bottle and went to find out what was wrong with it. And he said, yeah, it was pure poison. Something just hit me up before I drank it. He didn't drink me. He found out what it was. See?
Well, I guess a lot of people used to do all kind of things in those days.

Boysmen. Well, we had a guitar player. I'll forget that boy's name. But he had a knack of five or six women's at a dance with Jack Kerrin in. Playing at National Park. Boy, that was a jumping spot. And he danced five and six girls there. And he's bigoted like, you know. He's nice looking, but he's bigoted. I can't call his name. You go ahead, I'll see you tomorrow. You go ahead, I'll see you. And all that. Kept on with that stuff. But one of them guys, I pardoned him. He sold up like that. Don't nobody know what happened. Who killed him? Yeah, they pardoned the devil in them days, did you?
They said that about Buddy Bolden, too.

And there's another trumpet player. I didn't get the scene. But it's Buddy Bolden days. But I know, yes, I did get the scene. When I got the scene, he was paralyzed. And they say a woman told him he was going to kick her down the step in the condom home. And she told him if he kicked her down the step, he'll never use that arm and hand no more. And that's the truth. That leg either. He kicked her down the dog if he wasn't. Got a fella I've drunk ever since. Some old trumpet player. I don't know who he was. Yes, I do know his name, too. But I can't call it now.
Was he from Uptown or down?
Uptown. Tall dog guy.
Did you know Edward Clem?
It wasn't him.
Hot dog. That man named Ray Clem. It'll come to you later.
Yeah.
Did you play any excursions out of here?
I'm the only one who played them. Till I left in Lee College and played one. But I played all the booster excursions. Every time one went out, I was the guy that played it.
Where'd you go on those things?
Homer. On the Southern Pacific, you better say that. But the best excursions I ever played was from Chicago to Memphis.
Whose band was that? Your one?

Mine. Little made up band. Let me tell you what happened. I asked Francois who had the band. He wouldn't come, you know. None of them didn't want to come. So I got me a little made up band. And when we come, the boy, Charlie Allen, that was the man running. He asked them, did they want a wedding partnership or did they want a salary? No, man, no partnership. Let's give us $15 a man. Dick, they had a great big yard, see. And they pay at the gate. Down the quarter at the gate. And that yard was packed and jammed. The hall was packed and jammed. You couldn't get any, see. So he paid them the $15. Took them the five of them. And I worked with it. You see, I worked with it. And they paid all them orders. And they said, what you ready to give me, Dick?
What's that?

$305. Boy, I never made that much money before in my life. And did you know they got mad with me? And he asked them how did they want to wait. Asked them in front. Now that wasn't my fault, was it? No.
Well, people are jealous, you know.
That's right. They just figured we wasn't going to make nothing. And boy, I never seen so many people.
What did you do on the excursion?

Well, to take that baggage car, see. They got barrels of beer on the side. And they got gambling over there. And they got the space. You know, got them two doors barred off, you know, bars keep you from falling out. And we sat way up in the corner with the band. Them people danced like hell out there. And you got so many hours to play. You get so much for them hours and you come back, play so many more hours. We played from time to two to three o'clock in the morning. Just train running and we playing. Yeah. Yeah. That must have been good. That was good, Dick. All that stuff was good, partner. What kind of gambling games did they play? Huh? What kind of card games? They played poker. Mm-hm.
